annotations.text:
THE JOB OF THIS SCREEN

You told me three moments open Compare Prices: you are deciding who to buy from, a customer is standing there asking a price, and you are weighing your line against a rival product. TWO OF THOSE THREE ARE PRICING MOMENTS -- and you said that if the screen could answer only one question in its first 200px, it should be WHAT SHOULD I SELL IT AT.

Today "Sell at" is the SIXTH COLUMN of a six-column table, on the far right, below three stacked notes. The headline of the screen is about a supplier. So the screen answers, first and largest, a question you asked it third.

Everything on the proposal follows from four decisions.

1. THE ANSWER BAND IS THREE FIGURES, AND SELL AT IS FIRST. What to charge, what it costs you, and what the lot earns. That band is the whole counter conversation and the whole buying decision in 100px, and it is the first thing under the search. Both figures are INK, not colour: a price is a size, not a warning.

2. THE TWO VIEWS ARE NAMED AND SWITCHED, NOT SWAPPED. You said keep the rival-product matrix but make the switch obvious. It is now two tabs -- "Who sells it to you" and "Against other products" -- and the chips that pick the rivals live INSIDE the second view, where they belong. Today ticking a chip silently replaces one table with a completely different one and the only way back is to untick every chip.

3. THE ROW OPENS AND CARRIES THE WHOLE LADDER. A supplier's volume tiers are what a wholesaler actually negotiates on, and today the screen shows ONE rung of them, as a table cell reading "80 more -> 49,800". The open row draws all four rungs, marks the one you are standing on, and puts what you ACTUALLY PAID that supplier -- read from your own purchase invoices -- beside what they quoted.

4. THE ACCENT APPEARS ONCE, INSIDE THE OPEN ROW. One oxide button, on the one supplier you have opened. Everything else on the screen is ink and hairlines.

Everything is drawn from index.html's own values: the 23-colour palette, the 11/12/13/14 ramp, Inter + Archivo Black + IBM Plex Mono, and the .ow-* console components already shipping on Today, Debtors, Chase debts, Follow-ups, Consignment, Creditors and Pricing. No new colour, no new weight, no new type size, no fourteenth button family.

WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT AS IT STANDS >

The numbers on the drawing are these.

1. A 232-CHARACTER PARAGRAPH, UNMEASURED, ABOVE THE WORK. On a 1660px screen it runs past 180 characters a line. The console header is a name, one line, a hairline; the long version goes behind the "i". Seven screens already do this. This is one of the ones left.

2. THE SEARCH THAT IS THE WHOLE SCREEN IS 360px WIDE, AND IT CLIPS. .compare-select sets max-width:360px inside a 1140px panel, and it is an <input>, so "Iron sheets -- G28 box profile, 3m . charcoal grey" is cut to "...charcoal g" with no ellipsis, no marker and no way to read the rest. That is fault one of the truncation rule, and it is on the most important control on the page.

3. THE QUANTITY DECIDES WHO IS CHEAPEST AND IS DRESSED AS AN AFTERTHOUGHT. A 190px number box at the far right, and the unit beside it is read off the priced rows -- so before a product is chosen it is BLANK, and the box says "how many" of nothing.

4. THE RIVAL CHIPS SIT ABOVE THE RESULTS IN BOTH VIEWS AND SWAP THE TABLE SILENTLY. Ranking suppliers of one product and ranking products against each other are different questions with different answers. Nothing on screen says which one you are looking at.

5. THE VERDICT IS A 24px ARCHIVO BLACK SUPPLIER NAME ON AMBER. Archivo Black is for page names -- that is the whole of its job in this app. And the amber is doing double duty: it means "the best price is stale", but it reads as the screen's main colour.

6. UP TO FOUR STACKED NOTES BETWEEN THE VERDICT AND THE MONEY. The variant banner, the stale note, the undated note and the no-markup-rule note. Each is a true thing; none is ranked; together they push the ranking below the fold. Three of the four are drawn here.

7. THE "BEST" BADGE IS A FLAG-SHAPED VERDIGRIS TAG WITH A CSS TRIANGLE, AT 10.5px/700. Verdigris means GOOD in this app. Cheapest is not good, it is first. And the same badge is reused in the matrix reading "CHEAPEST", so one device carries two meanings.

8. THE MONEY DOES NOT LINE UP, AND IT IS NOT A NEAR MISS. renderCompare emits <th class="r"> on four columns and .price on the figures -- but NO th.r / td.r rule is in scope anywhere in the stylesheet, and .price sets no text-align. Every figure column in this table is LEFT-ALIGNED. The design system's rule is "right-aligned in every table"; a column of money that does not line up is unreadable at a glance, which is the only way it is read.

9. SELL AT IS THE LAST COLUMN ON THE RIGHT. The thing you told me should be the first answer is the last thing on the row, past four other columns.

10. THE PRICE LADDER IS INVISIBLE. cmpNextBreak finds the next rung that beats today's and shows it as one cell. A supplier with four tiers shows one of them, and nothing says whether that rung beats the WINNER. On this drawing it does: Ssekitoleko at 160 is 51,200, cheaper than the best price on the screen -- and the screen does not say so.

11. NOTHING TO DO. The screen ends at a table. Every other console screen in this app names the next action.

12. AMBER INK ON AN OXIDE FILL, IN THE SEARCH LIST. .suggestion-bulk-badge fills with var(--accent) and inks with var(--accent-ink) -- dark olive on red. The design system names this exact pairing as the worst thing shipped in the app and the reason the contrast test was written. Look at "ALL 4 SIZES" on the drawing: it is unreadable on a desk, never mind a phone in Ugandan sun.

AND OFF THE DRAWING:

13. NOTHING SAYS WHAT YOU ACTUALLY PAID. The app holds your purchase invoices; the Price Registry's Paid view reads them. Compare Prices ranks on QUOTES only, and cannot tell you the supplier it just recommended charged you 1,500 more than they quoted the last time you bought.

14. THE PHONE IS THE DESKTOP TABLE REFLOWED. .cmp-cards swaps the table for cards carrying the same three .sc-stat cells at the phone breakpoint. The two-designs law says 820px is a switch between two designs, not a reflow of one -- and the phone job here (a supplier on the line quoting you a figure) is not served at all.

THE PROPOSAL -- what changed, and why

SELL AT IS FIRST AND LARGEST, AND IT SHOWS ITS WORKING. 67,500, then the sentence that makes it checkable rather than trusted: cost 52,000, plus this line's wholesale rule of +30%, rounded to the nearest 500, and you keep 15,500 a sheet -- 23.0% of what the customer pays. That last clause matters and the app has never said it: a +30% MARKUP ON COST and a 23% MARGIN KEPT are different numbers, and the Pricing screen speaks in kept-% while this screen speaks in markup. Naming both in one line is the difference between a figure you obey and a figure you can argue with.

THE THIRD TILE IS THE ONE THAT SETTLES AN ARGUMENT AT THE COUNTER. The lot earns 1,860,000 at the suggested price -- and 1,680,000 at the 66,000 you actually charge today. The gap is the reason to change the price, in shillings, without anyone having to work it out.

ONE CAUTION, RANKED, INSTEAD OF FOUR NOTES. Only one thing on this screen changes the decision: 40 more sheets and Ssekitoleko is cheaper than the winner -- 8,192,000 against 8,320,000 for 160. It gets an amber band at the top of the ranking with the arithmetic in it and a way to act on it. The stale price, the undated price and the pallet-only supplier are not notes any more; they are the "Checked" column and the account at the foot.

THE ACCOUNT AT THE FOOT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PARAGRAPH ON THE SCREEN. 6 suppliers, 5 priced at 120, 1 by the pallet, 1 over ninety days old, 1 with no date -- so 2 of the 6 cannot be called current. That is the only device that lets you trust a ranking for what it does NOT say. Margin already does this and it is the best thing on that screen.

THE OPEN ROW IS THE WHOLE SUPPLIER. All four rungs of the ladder with the one you are standing on marked, and the next rung priced ("80 more saves 2,200 a sheet -- 440,000 across 200"). Then four supporting figures, then the finding that matters: the quote on file says 52,000, the last invoice charged 53,500, and the screen says which one it ranked on and what the answer would be on the other. Nothing in this app has ever put a quote and an invoice side by side.

THE RAIL CARRIES THE THREE THINGS YOU CANNOT DERIVE FROM THE RANKING. What you actually paid, from your own purchase invoices. What you charge today, and when it was last set. What the street charges, from the rival sightings already on file -- every figure something a person saw, with the day.

TRUNCATION IS DELIBERATE. The money columns are sized to their content and never give way; the supplier name is the column that yields, with the full value in the title. "1,240,00" is a tenth of "1,240,000" and looks entirely plausible, so a figure is never cut. The name may be.

HEIGHT: the paragraph, the banner and the three notes came to roughly 290px above the ranking. The answer band is 100px, and the winner's ladder, invoices and action are open on the first screen.

WHAT I HAVE NOT DECIDED FOR YOU

1. THE ACCENT'S ACTION. I have drawn "Order 120 from Mulongo", with the note that nothing is sent and it opens a purchase order with the quantity and the price filled in for you to confirm. That respects the law that nothing sends itself, but it is the one thing on this screen I invented rather than found. If you would rather it were "Take 67,500 to a quote" -- the counter moment rather than the buying one -- or nothing at all, say so; it is one button.

2. WHETHER THE RANKING SHOULD USE THE QUOTE OR THE INVOICE. Today it ranks on quotes, because that is what a supplier last SAID. The open row now shows that Mulongo charged 1,500 more than they quoted. Ranking on what people actually charge you would be a different screen and arguably a truer one. I have left the ranking alone and made the discrepancy visible instead, because changing it silently would be worse than either choice.

3. "SELLING THEM: BY THE SHEET" IS A NEW CONTROL. Today the wholesale-or-retail question is answered for you by whether the quantity clears the pack size (cmpKindAtQty), and the screen never says which rule it used. I have made it visible and changeable. If you would rather it stayed automatic, it becomes a line of text instead of a dropdown.

4. THE VOLUME PROMPT IS ONE RULE. "40 more and X is cheaper than the best" fires when another supplier's ladder crosses below the current winner within some distance of your quantity. I have drawn it at 33% more. Where that threshold sits is a real decision -- too loose and it fires on every line.

5. WHAT I HAVE NOT TOUCHED: rankedPurchaseRowsAtQty, purchasePriceAtQty, suggestedSellingPrice, cmpMatrix and the basis logic, the variant handling, or any figure. This is the same data, ranked the same way, drawn differently.

6. TWO THINGS THAT ARE BUGS RATHER THAN DESIGN, and want fixing whatever you decide here: the missing th.r/td.r rule that leaves every money column left-aligned, and the amber-on-oxide "ALL 4 SIZES" badge in the search list.

THE SECOND VIEW -- and why the switch had to be named >

You said keep it and make the switch obvious. So it is a tab, not a side effect, and the chips that choose the rivals moved INSIDE it. You can see at a glance which view you are in and get back in one tap without untangling four chips.

THE MATRIX'S REAL SUBJECT IS THE BASIS, NOT THE PRICE. cmpMatrix already works this out and the current screen already labels it -- that is the best idea on the whole screen and it is drawn as a 10px caption. Here it is a coloured line under each size, in words: "Per sheet -- exact", "Per bundle -- read with care", "Not comparable". Verdigris where the comparison is exact, amber where it is a bundle against a bundle, grey where it means nothing. That is colour that earns itself.

THE GALVANISED ROW IS THE POINT OF THE WHOLE DESIGN. Roofings quote a pallet with no sheet count on file, so NOTHING on this screen can say what one sheet costs -- and rather than dropping the row or guessing, it says so and names what would fix it. "Named rather than dropped" is one of this app's laws and this is the row that tests it.

THE THIRD TILE IS A CAVEAT, DELIBERATELY. "A cheaper sheet is not the same sheet. This compares price on a stated basis. It reads nothing about gauge, coating or who made it, and it does not judge the goods." G30 is thinner than G28 and that is exactly why it is cheaper -- but the app holds no field that knows it, so the screen must not imply it does. Derived, never invented.

WHAT I LEFT ALONE: the matching by variant name, the unmatched-sizes note, the per-piece / per-pack / per-unit machinery. All of it is right. It was just drawn at 9.5px in a table with left-aligned money.

THE THREE STATES A SCREEN IS ONLY DESIGNED ONCE YOU HAVE DRAWN >

1. NOTHING PICKED YET. Today: "Search and choose a product above to see who to buy it from." True, and it wastes the whole screen. This one names the job in a sentence, then offers the four lines you looked up last and says that What's worth buying has 9 lines waiting on a price. Both are derived -- from your own search history and from the plan the app already builds -- so the empty screen is a way in rather than a wall. And there is NO strip of zeros: four tiles reading 0 is four figures that mean nothing.

2. A PRODUCT WITH NOTHING ON FILE. Today: "No prices recorded yet for this product." This one adds the two facts the app already holds and that make it actionable -- you have sold 34 of them in 30 days at 18,000, so the shop knows what it charges but nothing knows what it costs -- and names the next action rather than describing the absence.

3. THE STATE THAT DOES NOT EXIST TODAY. If the Price Registry fails to read, renderCompare falls through to the same "No prices recorded yet for this product" as a genuinely new line. A failed read and an empty shelf are not the same news, and only one of them is yours to fix. The app's own law says a failure must name itself: so it says what failed, when the last good read was and what it held, that those figures are NOT current and are not being shown, and it turns the suggested selling price off. A price set on figures nobody can see is a price set blind.

THE PHONE -- its own design, not the table reflowed

820px is a switch, so this is drawn from scratch at 390: 44px navy bar, 26px page name, 15px body, 48px controls, no fake status bar and no fake keyboard.

THE PHONE JOB IS NOT THE DESK JOB. At the desk you are working through suppliers before placing an order. On a phone, a supplier has just said a figure down the line, or somebody in the yard is asking what a thing costs. Both are answered by TWO NUMBERS -- what you would pay and what to sell at -- so those two come first, at 24px, and the ranking is under them. The sub says it out loud: "Somebody has quoted you a figure. Is it a good one?"

THE QUANTITY IS A STEPPER. It is the control that decides who is cheapest, and a number typed into a phone in a yard is a mis-tap waiting to happen. 48px targets either side of the figure.

THE CARDS CARRY NO BUTTON. Four oxide buttons on a screen allowed one accent is no accent. The accent lives once, in the docked navy bar in the thumb zone -- the pattern Follow-ups, Debtors, Creditors and Pricing already ship -- and it names the default action so it is right without reading the list.

THE ACCOUNT SURVIVES, SHORTENED. "6 suppliers on file. 5 priced at 120. 2 cannot be called current." Same three facts as the desk, one line.

ONE THING TO DECIDE: whether the phone should be able to START AN ORDER at all, or only read. I have drawn "Open it" rather than a send, and the bar says "nothing is sent" -- but if you would rather the phone were strictly a lookup, the dock becomes a "Copy the price" and the order stays on the desk.
